claims.text: A tailored tempering heat treatment can promote phosphorus or antimony segregation at grain boundaries in conventional tempered martensitic steel.
The treated martensitic steel will exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition over a narrow temperature window.
Precise control of tempering temperature and hold time encourages impurity segregation at grain boundaries.
The steel is inherently ductile at high testing temperatures.
Impurity mobility at intermediate temperatures causes segregation and embrittlement.
At low temperatures, impurity mobility becomes frozen and ductility recovers.
Phosphorus or antimony segregates at the grain boundaries of the treated steel.
Impurities migrate to grain boundaries during tailored tempering.
Grain-boundary impurity segregation reduces grain-boundary cohesive strength.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesive strength causes a marked loss of ductility within a narrow temperature window.
Further cooling freezes the impurity distribution and permits ductility to recover.
The treated steel will have high ductility at elevated temperatures.
The treated steel will become brittle within a narrow intermediate temperature range.
The treated steel will recover ductility at lower temperatures.
Untreated conventional tempered martensitic steel does not display a pronounced ductile–brittle–ductile transition over a narrow temperature window.
The proposed effect is sensitive to impurity concentration, tempering temperature, and hold time.
Large deviations in impurity concentration or heat-treatment parameters may prevent observable temper embrittlement.
